title: CAP Theorem
subtitle: When the network splits, you must choose — and you don't get to choose whether to choose
objectives: State CAP precisely, and explain why 'pick two of three' is a misleading slogan
Explain why partition tolerance isn't optional and what the real choice is
Work out what CP and AP actually feel like for a user
Apply the real-world version: the tradeoff exists even when the network is healthy

exercises.title: A partition leaves a node exactly two options, and both of them are bad
exercises.body: The link between two datacenters drops. Every machine is up; every user still reaches one side or the other. That's a *partition*, and it puts a node in a strange position: its own copy is now the only evidence it has, and it cannot tell whether the world has moved on without it. Then a read arrives. It has two possible answers, and only two.
exercises.note: So the theorem is narrower than the slogan. It isn't offering three properties to shop among — it describes one node's options at a moment when the network has already decided something for you.

exercises.prompt: Two datacenters hold copies of your data. The network link between them fails, but both are alive and users are hitting both. A user writes to datacenter A. What can datacenter B do about it?
choices: Nothing — it cannot hear about the write, so it must either serve data it knows might be stale, or refuse to answer
exercises.why: B has no way to learn about A's write while the link is down, so it faces two options and only two: answer with what it has and risk being wrong, or refuse to answer until it can be sure. That fork is the entire content of CAP — it isn't a theory about database vendors, it's what physically remains possible when two machines cannot talk.

exercises.prompt: Match each letter of CAP to what it means.

pairs.right: Every read sees the most recent write
Every request gets a non-error response
The system keeps working when the network splits
Nodes alive, but unable to reach each other

exercises.why: Note that CAP's Consistency is a stricter thing than ACID's C from unit 9 — here it means reads reflect the latest write, not 'your constraints hold'. Same letter, different promise, and conflating them has confused engineers for two decades.

exercises.prompt: CAP is usually taught as 'pick two of three'. Why is that misleading?
choices: Because you can actually have all three
Because partitions aren't a design choice — networks fail whether you like it or not, so P isn't something you can decline
Because there are really four properties
Because it only applies to NoSQL
exercises.why: You can't opt out of the network failing any more than you can opt out of weather, so 'choosing CA' really means 'choosing to have no plan for a partition' — which isn't a design, it's an omission. The honest statement is narrower and more useful: WHEN a partition happens, you must choose between consistency and availability. The rest of the time the question isn't being asked.

exercises.prompt: So what does a 'CA system' actually describe?
choices: A single node — no partition is possible when there's nothing to partition from. Distributed systems don't get this option
exercises.why: Partitions are a property of having more than one machine, so the only genuine CA system is one that isn't distributed at all — which is a real and often excellent choice, and it's exactly the single box unit 11 defended. The moment you add a second machine you've bought into P, and with it the choice you now have to make deliberately.

exercises.prompt: A network ______ is when nodes are alive but can't reach each other.
exercises.why: The nodes are healthy and doing their jobs — it's the path between them that's broken, which is what makes it so much nastier than a clean crash. A dead node stops answering; a partitioned node keeps happily answering, with a view of the world that's drifting away from its peers.

exercises.prompt: During a partition, why can't a node just tell whether it's the one that's cut off?
choices: It can — it checks its network card
It can't: from inside, 'the other node is dead', 'the other node is slow', and 'I am the one who's isolated' all look identical
exercises.why: All a node observes is silence, and silence has many causes it cannot distinguish — this is the same undecidable 'dead or just slow?' from units 10 and 12, which is why it keeps reappearing. A partition doesn't announce itself; both sides just notice the other has gone quiet, and each may conclude it's the survivor.

exercises.title: A CP system would rather be down than be wrong
exercises.body: Choosing consistency means choosing to refuse. When the network splits, a node that cannot confirm it holds the latest data has exactly one honest move left, and it is not to guess. So perfectly healthy machines stop serving. Nobody reads a wrong value there because nobody reads at all. That isn't the design failing; it *is* the design.
exercises.note: But *which* side stops? Both look identical from the inside, so the rule can't rely on either one knowing it's the odd one out. It has to be a test that only one side of any split can pass — arithmetic, not judgement.

exercises.prompt: A partition splits your cluster. You choose consistency. What does a user on the minority side experience?
choices: Errors or timeouts — the system refuses to serve rather than risk answering with data it can't verify
Their writes queue up and apply later
exercises.why: Choosing consistency means choosing to fail rather than to guess, so a node that can't confirm it has the latest data must decline — and 'decline' is what the user sees as an error. That's the honest shape of CP: the system stays correct by becoming partly unavailable, and the unavailability is the mechanism, not a bug in it.

exercises.prompt: How does a CP system decide which side of a partition may keep serving?
choices: A quorum — the side holding a majority of nodes can proceed, and the minority steps back, because only one side can hold a majority
The side with the newest data
exercises.why: Majority is the trick that makes it safe: with an odd number of nodes, at most one side of any split can have more than half, so a quorum rule guarantees the two sides can never both believe they're in charge. That's precisely the split-brain from unit 10 being prevented by arithmetic instead of hope — and it's why cluster sizes are odd, since 3 tolerates one failure while 4 tolerates exactly the same one and costs more.

exercises.prompt: 5-node cluster, quorum of 3. A partition leaves 3 nodes on one side and 2 on the other. What happens?
choices: The 3-node side has a majority and continues; the 2-node side must stop accepting writes even though those nodes are perfectly healthy
exercises.why: The minority nodes aren't broken — they're working fine and simply can't prove they aren't missing writes, so they must stand down. This is CP's bargain stated plainly: you deliberately give up capacity that physically exists in order to guarantee no one is served a wrong answer. Users on the minority side are down, and that's the design working.

exercises.prompt: Which systems should lean CP? Select all.
choices: A view counter on a video
exercises.why: Money, stock, and locks share a property: a wrong answer creates a real-world commitment you can't take back — you've double-spent, oversold, or handed the same lock to two owners. Refusing to answer is recoverable; answering wrongly isn't. A view counter is the opposite, where being briefly wrong costs nothing at all.

exercises.prompt: A distributed lock service goes AP — both sides of a partition keep granting locks. What breaks?
choices: Two clients hold 'the same' lock simultaneously, which destroys the only property a lock exists to provide
exercises.why: A lock's entire value is that exactly one holder exists, so a lock service that stays available during a partition by granting both sides isn't a degraded lock — it's not a lock. This is the clearest case where availability is worthless: an always-available service that doesn't do its job has no reason to exist, which is why lock services are firmly CP and simply go down rather than lie.

exercises.prompt: What's the real cost of choosing CP?
choices: Downtime for anyone who can't reach a quorum — you've converted a network problem into a visible outage, on purpose
exercises.why: CP doesn't make the partition go away, it decides who suffers from it: instead of quiet wrong answers you get loud errors, which are far easier to notice and reason about. That's a genuine feature — a system that fails visibly is one you can respond to — but be clear that you chose an outage, and a user staring at an error doesn't care that it was principled.

exercises.title: An AP system always has an answer — it just might not be *the* answer
exercises.body: Choosing availability means choosing to answer anyway. Both sides of a split keep serving from their own copies, so nobody gets an error and some people get data missing the other side's writes. The real cost isn't the stale read, though. It's whatever the two sides have quietly accumulated by the time the network comes back.
exercises.note: And you will have a merge rule whether you write one or not. Every system has a default — and defaults are chosen by whoever wrote the library, never by whoever understands what your data actually means.

exercises.prompt: Same partition, but you choose availability. What does the user on the minority side experience?
choices: A normal response — served from that node's own copy, which may be missing writes that happened on the other side
exercises.why: AP keeps answering with local knowledge, so nobody sees an error and some people see the past — the failure moves from visible to invisible. That's often exactly right: for a social feed, a comment appearing a few seconds late is nothing, while an error page is a real problem the user will actually notice and resent.

exercises.prompt: During an AP partition, users on both sides edit the same record. The network heals. What now?
choices: The system picks the correct one automatically
You have two divergent versions and must reconcile them — and there's no universally right answer for which edit should win
The later timestamp is always correct
exercises.why: AP's bill comes due at healing time: both sides accepted writes in good faith, so you now hold two histories and must merge them with rules you invented. 'Last write wins' is the common choice and it silently discards someone's work — and it leans on clocks from different machines agreeing, which is its own well-known trap.

exercises.prompt: Match each conflict resolution strategy.

pairs.right: Simple — and silently destroys one edit
Push the choice to the user or app
Structure the data so merges can't conflict

exercises.why: The choice depends entirely on what the data means, which is why no database can solve it for you. Notice the last row: an operation expressed as 'add this item' merges cleanly from both sides, while the same intent expressed as 'the cart now contains N' cannot — so how you model the write decides whether conflicts are resolvable at all.

exercises.prompt: Why is a shopping cart the classic AP example?
choices: Amazon reasoned that a customer being unable to add to cart is a lost sale, while a rare merge oddity is a recoverable annoyance — availability was worth more than perfect consistency
exercises.why: The reasoning is about business cost rather than technology: refusing an add-to-cart is revenue that vanishes, and a resurrected item is something the customer can just remove at checkout. Notice they didn't abandon consistency everywhere — the actual purchase and payment are far stricter. Different data in the same system gets different answers, because different data has a different cost of being wrong.

exercises.prompt: Which systems reasonably lean AP? Select all.
choices: An account balance shown before a transfer
exercises.why: Feeds, DNS, and like counts all tolerate being briefly behind — DNS is aggressively AP by design, which is why a record change takes time to propagate and nobody considers that a bug. A balance is different: showing a stale number right before someone commits to a transfer invites a decision they'd not have made, so staleness there has a real cost.

exercises.prompt: What's the real cost of choosing AP?
choices: Some users act on stale data, and after the partition heals you own a reconciliation problem that no library can decide for you
Nothing — AP is strictly better for user experience
exercises.why: AP trades a visible failure now for a silent divergence you must resolve later, which is genuinely the better trade for a lot of data — and the cost is real and lands somewhere quieter. Nobody gets paged, so the wrongness lives in your data rather than your dashboard, and the merge rules are a design decision you'll be making with tired hands after the incident if you don't make them now.

exercises.title: The theorem describes a rare emergency, not the system you run every day
exercises.body: CAP is a statement about partitions, and only about partitions. That should bother you more than it does: your network is fine almost all of the time, so for almost your system's whole life the theorem is silent. So what constrains you the rest of the time? Something has to make a node's answer *correct*, and that something has a price.
exercises.note: That something is coordination: a node can't know it holds the latest write without asking someone who might. How far the ask goes, how many it waits for — that's the design you operate. CAP is what you rehearse for.

exercises.prompt: Your network is healthy — no partition at all. Does CAP say anything about your system right now?
choices: Yes — you must still pick two
No — CAP only constrains you DURING a partition. With a healthy network you can have both consistency and availability
exercises.why: CAP is a statement about one specific failure mode, and outside it the theorem is simply silent — which is why 'we're an AP system' as a permanent identity is a category error. The right reading is conditional: when a partition happens, here's what we do. The other 99.9% of the time, that choice isn't being exercised at all.

exercises.prompt: So if CAP is silent when the network is fine, what tradeoff still exists during normal operation?
choices: Latency versus consistency: to be strongly consistent you must coordinate with other nodes, and coordination costs a round trip on every operation
exercises.why: Confirming you have the latest data means asking someone else, and asking someone else takes time — so strong consistency is bought with latency on the happy path, every single day. This is what PACELC adds to CAP: else (no partition), you're trading Latency against Consistency, which is the tradeoff you actually live with continuously rather than during rare failures.

exercises.prompt: Why does that latency-vs-consistency tradeoff matter more day to day than CAP itself?
choices: Because partitions are rare while every request pays the coordination cost, so the everyday tradeoff shapes your system far more than the rare one
Because latency is easier to measure
exercises.why: You'll meet a partition a handful of times a year and the coordination cost on every request today — so a design chosen entirely around CAP optimizes for the rare case while ignoring the constant one. That's also unit 4's physics reasserting itself: a cross-region quorum means waiting for a machine 150ms away, and no protocol negotiates with the speed of light.

exercises.prompt: You're designing 'number of people currently viewing this page'. A partition splits your cluster. Slide toward your choice.
exercises.leftLabel: CP — refuse rather than show a wrong count
exercises.why: The count is decorative: nobody makes a decision from it, and being off by a few during a partition costs precisely nothing, while an error where a number should be looks broken. This is the whole method — ask what a wrong answer actually costs, and here it costs less than no answer. Run the same question on a bank balance and you'll slide to the opposite end.

exercises.prompt: A vendor says their database is 'CA — no compromises'. What should you conclude?
choices: It's marketing: either it's a single node, or it silently picks CP or AP during a partition and isn't telling you which
It's the right choice for everything
exercises.why: Nobody has repealed the theorem, so a distributed 'CA' system is one that hasn't told you its behaviour during a partition — and that behaviour exists whether documented or not. The question worth asking a vendor is concrete: during a partition, does the minority side serve reads, and what happens to writes? A good answer is specific; a bad one repeats the marketing.

exercises.prompt: Should one system pick CP or AP for all its data?
choices: No — different data has different costs of being wrong, so the same product can be CP for payments and AP for the activity feed
Yes — the database decides for you
exercises.why: CAP applies per operation and per dataset rather than per company, and treating it as an identity forces every piece of data to inherit the strictness that only your money needed. Real systems mix deliberately: strict where a wrong answer creates an irreversible commitment, relaxed where staleness is a shrug — which is the same 'what does being wrong cost?' question that has run through every unit since state.

exercises.prompt: What's the honest summary of CAP?
choices: During a partition you must choose between refusing to answer and risking a stale answer — and the rest of the time, the live tradeoff is consistency against latency
exercises.why: CAP isn't a menu, it's a constraint that activates during a specific failure and forces a choice you'd rather not make — with PACELC's 'else' clause covering the far more common case where you're paying coordination latency instead. What both really say is that the network is a real, physical thing, and any design pretending otherwise is choosing its failure mode by accident.
